description: Stellar Innovators is a team of students passionate about space, technology, and innovation. We combine AI, Machine Learning, Data Analysis, Software Development, and creative problem-solving to turn NASA data into impactful solutions. We are looking for motivated teammates skilled in AI, Data, Development, Design, Research, and Storytelling who are ready to collaborate, learn, and build something remarkable together.
summary:
Delta Pulse is an open, bilingual (English and Arabic) web map of the changing Nile Delta. The Delta holds most
of Egypt's farmland and tens of millions of people on low, soft ground. It faces five linked hazards that are
usually studied in separate papers: land subsidence, cities spreading onto farmland, coastal erosion, sea-level rise
and loss of stored water. Delta Pulse puts them on one interactive map built on NASA data, led by the new
NISAR L-band radar mission.
We processed 17 provisional NISAR interferograms (June–October 2026) and show NISAR and Sentinel-1 radar
imagery on the map. We also computed four results from NASA data: sea level off the Delta rose 3.51 ± 0.62
mm/yr (1993–2018); water storage over the Delta fell 0.28 ± 0.02 cm/yr (2003–2021); shoreline change from 2016
to 2026 by coastal sector; and 6,647 km² of land exposed to a 1 m sea-level rise. Every value sits next to the
published value it is checked against. Four months of NISAR data do not yet resolve city subsidence, and the site
says so plainly.
Planners, engineers, students and the public can explore the map, follow a five-chapter story, and ask an AI
interpreter that answers only from the site's own numbers.
details:
The Delta Pulse website: the Nile Delta on NASA satellite imagery.

Delta Pulse answers one question for the Nile Delta: where is the land under pressure, and why? It shows five layers on one map of the Delta, from Cairo to the Mediterranean coast (29.5–32.6°E, 30.0–31.7°N): 

  1. Land subsidence: NISAR L-band interferograms (our first look) beside published long-term rates for 12 cities. 
  2. Urban expansion: NISAR and Sentinel-1 radar imagery and a 2016 ⇄ 2026 optical swipe. 
  3. Coastal erosion: 2016 and 2026 shorelines and rates of change measured on 462 transects. 
  4. Sea-level rise: the sea-level trend off the Delta and maps of land exposed at +0.25, +0.5 and +1.0 m. 
  5. Water storage: GRACE/GRACE-FO trends for the Delta, the Western Desert and Sinai. 

The site explains how the hazards connect. Pumped groundwater and the weight of cities compact the soft ground, so the land sinks. Sinking land adds to the rising sea, and a coast with little river sediment retreats. One published example carries the story: at New Damietta the sea rises 3.42 mm/yr, but the tide gauge on land records 8.21 mm/yr, because the land under it sinks (Hassan et al. 2025). Our own sea-level trend plus the published land motion gives 7.3 ± 0.9 mm/yr, which agrees with the tide gauge.

How to try it (for judges) 

  1. Open https://delta-pulse-web.vercel.app. The opening sequence flies from the globe to the Delta; press Skip to go straight to the map. 
  2. Explore: choose a layer in the left panel. Try "Coastal erosion" and drag the 2016 ⇄ 2026 divider, or "Sea-level rise" and switch between 0.25, 0.5 and 1.0 m. 
  3. Click any place on the map. The right panel shows the values for that point and the source of each number. 
  4. Story: five short chapters in causal order (groundwater → subsidence → cities → sea → coast). 
  5. Data & limits: our value next to the published value for each result, the dataset list, and the caveats. 
  6. Ask the interpreter: for example "Why is Damietta at risk?" in English or Arabic. It answers only from the site's numbers and names their sources. 
  7. Use the language switch for the full Arabic (right-to-left) version, and the Simple ⇄ Scientist switch for more detail. 

How it works 

  • Data pipeline (Python). Scripts in the pipeline folder produce every number we show. Each output file records its method, source, period and caveats. 
  • NISAR interferometry. We read 17 consecutive 12-day NISAR GUNW pairs on two tracks (129 ascending, 007 descending), about 37 GB in total. We kept the largest connected component, masked coherence below 0.7, tested four ionosphere and troposphere correction options for each pair, converted phase to line-of-sight millimetres, and fitted rates. Each city (2.5 km radius) is measured against its surrounding ring (6–15 km) to remove water-vapour patches. 
  • Reading NASA GIBS tiles as data. For sea level, GRACE and surface water, we turn the colours of NASA GIBS map tiles back into values through their published colour tables. This needs no login and no bulk download. Values are exact to the colour bin (1 cm for sea level, 0.25 cm for GRACE). 
  • Trends. Linear trend fitted together with annual and semi-annual cycles. The standard error is corrected for autocorrelation. 
  • Shoreline. Seasonal water composites (June–September 2016 and 2026) from OPERA DSWx-HLS, with shore-normal transects every 500 m. 
  • Flood exposure. Copernicus DEM at 90 m. Land counts as exposed only when it is at or below the sea level and connected to the sea. 
  • Web app. A static site (Vite, plain JavaScript, MapLibre GL JS on a globe, three.js for the opening sequence) with NASA GIBS tiles loaded live. A small server function sends interpreter questions to Claude (Anthropic API). The key stays on the server, and requests are rate-limited. 
  • Citation-first check. An automated check rejects any value of ours that does not name the script and the output file that produced it.

Figure 3. Processing workflow: three open NASA data streams are retrieved, analysed and written to self-describing files. An automated check admits only values that can be traced to a script and an output file. 

What works now 

  • The live site with all five layers, story mode, click-for-evidence panel, data page, English and Arabic, and the Simple and Scientist views. 
  • Four results computed by our pipeline and checked against published values (section 6). 
  • The NISAR first look on two tracks, with its uncertainty shown. 
  • The AI interpreter, which answers in English or Arabic from the site's own numbers. 
  • A 14-page research manuscript that explains the methods and findings (section 7). 
  • Automated tests of the app and of the data rules. 

Limitations (stated in the app) 

  • NISAR products are provisional and will be reprocessed in 2027. Four months of data are too short to measure subsidence of a few mm/yr; the NISAR layer is a first look. 
  • Interferometry measures motion along the radar's line of sight, relative to a reference. Our city values are relative to their surroundings. 
  • GRACE resolution is about 300 km, larger than the Delta. It shows total water storage, not groundwater alone. 
  • The shoreline comes from optical data, so tide and waves affect it, and changes below about 3 m/yr are not resolved. 
  • Flood exposure is a screening scenario, not a forecast. The elevation model is accurate to metres and has no sea walls or drains. 
  • The urban layer shows imagery only; we have not yet computed built-up change. 
  • The causes of subsidence are hypotheses from published studies, not results of our work. 

Future plans 

  • Add NISAR pairs after 21 October 2026 as they are released; with one to two years of data, city rates should reach about 2 mm/yr. 
  • Process a redundant interferogram network and better troposphere corrections. 
  • Compute built-up change 2016 → 2026 from OPERA RTC-S1 and NISAR backscatter. 
  • Remove soil moisture (GLDAS) from GRACE to isolate groundwater. 
  • Rank bridges, canals and sea defences on steep subsidence gradients for inspection. 

Benefits and intended impact 

  • Planners and ministries: one map that shows which areas sink, which coasts retreat and which land is low enough to flood. 
  • Engineers: coastal transects that are still eroding 10–12 m/yr, and a path to ranking structures on steep subsidence gradients. 
  • Researchers and students: a reproducible NISAR workflow for a delta, with open code and every number traced to its source. 
  • The public and journalists: the story in plain Arabic and English, with no radar training needed. 

Tools, languages and software 

Python (NumPy, SciPy, h5py, pyproj, Pillow, tifffile, imagecodecs); JavaScript (Vite, MapLibre GL JS 6, three.js, Vitest); Node.js; Anthropic Claude API for the interpreter; ElevenLabs for narration; Vercel for hosting. 

What is creative 

  • Five hazards that are usually studied apart, joined in one causal story on one map. 
  • One of the first L-band (NISAR) interferometry looks at the Nile Delta. The studies we reviewed used C-band radar. 
  • Reading NASA GIBS map tiles as data, so a small team can compute trends without logins or bulk downloads. 
  • A citation-first rule enforced in code: no number on the site without a script or a paper behind it. 
  • A fully bilingual interface for the people who live in the Delta. 

Factors we considered 

Honesty about uncertainty, so the site shows a negative result instead of a false signal. Low bandwidth, so we read subsets and tiles instead of whole files. Arabic first-class, not a translation layer. Accessibility: reduced-motion support and Skip on the opening sequence. No credentials in the browser. 

5. Key equations 

Trend model (sea level and water storage): a linear trend b plus annual and semi-annual cycles, with t in years. 

y(t) = a + b·t + Σₖ₌₁² [ cₖ·cos(2πkt) + sₖ·sin(2πkt) ] 

Effective sample size. The residuals are autocorrelated, so the trend error uses n_eff instead of n. For sea level, r₁ = 0.848 and n = 948 give n_eff = 78.1. 

n_eff = n · (1 − r₁) / (1 + r₁) 

Radar phase to ground motion along the line of sight (NISAR L-band, λ ≈ 0.24 m). Negative values mean motion away from the satellite, which for subsidence is downward. 

d = −(λ / 4π) · φ 

Track consistency test between the ascending rate a and the descending rate b. This tests consistency, not resolution: two noisy estimates can agree because their errors are large. 

|a − b| ≤ 2 · √(σa² + σb²) 

How long NISAR must observe. Rate error for acquisitions spaced Δt over a span T, each with independent error σ. Scaling today's 7.9–26.6 mm/yr from T ≈ 0.33 yr gives about 2 mm/yr after 0.8–1.9 years. 

σb ≈ σ · √(12·Δt) · T^(−3/2) 

Relative sea-level budget at New Damietta. Our sea-level trend plus the published InSAR land motion matches the tide gauge (8.21 ± 1.1 mm/yr). 

3.51 + 3.8 = 7.3 ± 0.9 mm/yr

 Figure 6. Mean coherence of the eight descending-track NISAR interferograms, June–October 2026 (white = high). Phase is kept over towns and villages, and lost over lagoons, fish farms and much of the farmland. 

Figure 7. City-relative line-of-sight rates from both NISAR tracks with ±1σ errors. The shaded band spans published rates for Delta cities (−2.4 to −20 mm/yr). 

How to read the NISAR result. The errors are as large as, or larger than, the published rates, so no city rate is resolved yet. At Mansoura and Alexandria the two tracks disagree in sign; the ascending track implies uplift, which points to water-vapour and soil-moisture phase errors. A city sinking 3–20 mm/yr moves only about 1–7 mm in four months. This honest negative result shows how long the NISAR record must be, and which corrections it needs. 

7. Research paper

We wrote up the methods and findings as a 14-page research manuscript in journal form:

"An Open Multi-Hazard Assessment of the Nile Delta from NASA Data, with a First Look at NISAR L-Band Interferometry"

Ali A. Khalil, Dyeie H. Hamid and Ahmed S. Ellaban, College of Computer Science, Damietta University

It covers the study area, data, every processing step with its equations, the results with figures and tables, a comparison with published studies, the physical drivers, and an estimate of how long the NISAR record must be before city subsidence can be measured.

Read it: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1gWuh_WPNcdUNIfte8YPWRC2yJaXd56CS/view
